narrative: The model estimated a 72.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, and because that risk was considered too high, your law school application was denied. The strongest reason was your third-year class standing: you were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. That large gap pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year class standing was the second most important factor, and it also worked against you: you were again in the lowest decile, compared with an accepted-student average near the sixth decile. Together, these two academic signals suggested sustained difficulty relative to admitted students. Your LSAT score was the third most influential factor. At 35 it was somewhat below the accepted average of 37.18, but in this case it slightly favored passing rather than failure, so it eased the risk only modestly and did not outweigh the academic concerns. To improve your chances, ask admissions for feedback, discuss whether any circumstances affected your early grades, and develop a concrete plan to strengthen your academic record. Consider retaking the LSAT if practice scores suggest meaningful improvement, and reapply only after you can show stronger evidence of bar-exam readiness.
